## Research {#research}

::: {.entry}
[The Frequency Term Structure of Equity Factors]{.entry-title}

[with Ingmar Nolte and Sandra Nolte]{.entry-authors}
[Work in progress · Presented at the 5th Frontiers of Factor Investing Conference (2026)]{.entry-status}

Empirical asset pricing studies almost always fix a single sampling frequency per analysis. This paper asks how the equity factor structure changes with the frequency at which returns are measured, from one second to one month, using a new high-frequency zoo of 662 factors built from 5,961 U.S. stocks (2014–2024).

<details>
<summary>Full abstract</summary>

Empirical asset pricing studies almost always fix a single sampling frequency per analysis. Monthly returns dominate the classical literature, daily returns are common, and a high-frequency strand works at sub-hour horizons, but in each case the analysis is conducted at one frequency only. This paper asks how the equity factor structure changes with the frequency at which returns are measured, and answers the question by tracing the term structure of Fama–MacBeth betas and risk premia for the Fama–French six-factor model (FF6) and the Jensen–Kelly–Pedersen factor zoo (JKP) across a dense grid of sampling frequencies spanning seven orders of magnitude in time, from one second to one calendar month, plus a dedicated overnight series, estimated on a novel high-frequency factor zoo of 662 factors built from 5,961 U.S. common stocks over 2014–2024. We implement the classical Shanken-corrected Fama–MacBeth procedure alongside the large-*N* bias-adjusted WLS estimator of Raponi, Robotti, and Zaffaroni with formal specification testing and a centred cross-sectional *R*² at every frequency, and we derive a closed-form rebalancing-drag correction that strips a mechanical compounding wedge out of cross-frequency lambda comparisons. Preliminary findings: the factor structure is not scale-invariant; the market factor and momentum are priced across the bulk of the term structure while HML, CMA, and RMW are not; the daily frequency appears to be a meaningful break in the factor structure; and the overnight regime is qualitatively different from either of its adjacent regimes.

[**Keywords:** factor models; Fama–MacBeth; high-frequency data; term structure; rebalancing drag; stochastic portfolio theory. **JEL:** G12, G14, C21, C58.]{.entry-keywords}

</details>
:::
